newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: MOLDOVANS VOTE, PRESIDENT'S RIVAL FEARS TROUBLE.
newsitem.headline: MOLDOVANS VOTE, PRESIDENT'S RIVAL FEARS TROUBLE.

text.p: Moldovans voted in the second round of the former Soviet republic's first multi-candidate presidential election on Sunday, as the left-wing challenger accused President Mircea Snegur of plotting to rig the ballot.
"People have been paid to vote. Other inventions to falsify the results are being used," candidate and parliament chairman Petru Lucinschi said after voting in the capital, Chisinau.
But Snegur, president since independence in 1991, hit back, accusing his opponent of dirty tricks.

Lucinschi, whom polls show running neck-and-neck with Snegur in the run-off after scoring 28 percent in the first round on November 17, also told reporters he feared Snegur's supporters could take to the streets, aided by the police.
Reporters saw no gatherings by early afternoon, however.
Foreign observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) reported no significant violations.

In the picturesque but run-down village of Tintareni -- the name comes from the Romanian for "mosquito" -- observers for both candidates said they foresaw no irregularities. Voters and officials seemed happy to drown their bitter campaign disputes together in copious glasses of fruity local wine.
National turnout by 3 p.m. (1300 GMT) was 41 percent. Some 2.4 million voters among the 4.3 million population have until 8 p.m. to vote. First results are expected during the night.

OSCE coordinator Kare Vollan told Reuters his observers were paying particular attention to polling stations close to the Russian-speaking Dnestr region, which broke away in 1990 fearing Moldovans wanted to unite with ethnic kin in Romania.
Authorities in the area, where hundreds died in fighting in 1992, are ignoring the poll but say local people can vote elsewhere. Only a few thousand did so in the first round.
Snegur on Sunday accused Lucinschi, whose backers range from state television and newspapers to the Orthodox Church, of "illegal methods, including mudslinging in the press, libel and rumours".
Pledging to press on with market reforms, the 56-year-old Snegur polled 39 percent in the first round and has since been endorsed by pro-Romanian nationalists.

But he faces stiff opposition. Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, knocked out in the first round, and the communists, support Lucinschi. Sangheli says he will resign after the election "to preserve civil peace".
The president's bluff down-to-earth image generally plays well in the countryside. But the economic crisis of the past five years has fuelled support for the intellectual Lucinschi.
In Tintareni, which backed the president solidly a fortnight ago, a majority of a dozen or so voters interviewed said they wanted Lucinschi to win a four-year term.
"Snegur is to blame for the war in Dnestr and the economic problems," said Vasile, 34 and unemployed. His Russian-speaking wife had not received her nurse's pay for four months.
But there is no shortage of Snegur loyalists.
"I'm for Snegur. He gave us our independence, he knows what to do," said Glavia, a Chisinau housewife in her 40s. "The problem is the government don't let him to what he needs to."

Snegur wants greater presidential powers to carry out reforms. He dismisses fears among the one-third Russian minority that he might unite with Romania, from whose territory Stalin carved most of Moldova in World War Two.
Lucinschi, also 56 and like the president a top communist in Soviet times, presents himself as a social democrat.

He accuses Snegur of seeking vast powers in the manner of Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko and of stirring up the Dnestr war. Playing down links with Bucharest, he reminds Moldovans they depend on Russia for their energy and much else.
